correctness.rationale: Two independent finite enumerations cover all 20,306 coefficient planes. A quartic discriminant formula and an independent polynomial-gcd criterion agree on 600 squarefree projective quartics and 3,820 pencils. The 120-element source PGL2 action is exhausted with unique RREF representatives and yields 47 disjoint orbits of the stated sizes. Independent gcd and polynomial-factor tests agree on the 3,710/70/40 common-divisor distribution and all fourteen rational-fibre Frobenius profiles. The mathematical link from a squarefree quartic to a four-point branch divisor and from a basepoint-free pencil to a degree-four separable rational morphism holds in characteristic five. The 40 degree-three-base pencils also admit an elementary irreducible-cubic count.

originality.rationale: Wall (1998) is direct same-object prior work, but its complex-geometric stratification and invariant theory do not supply the fixed-field all-six-squarefree census, the precise source-PGL2 orbit count or complete arithmetic splitting profiles. Asgarli–Ghioca (2022) concerns general existence of smooth pencils, not the exact binary-quartic F5 distribution. Published finite-field cubic-pencil orbit work classifies degree three, not four. Relevant searches and accessible deduplication records did not reveal a stronger covering computation. Priority remains qualified because an unindexed finite-field enumeration could exist.

value.rationale: The arithmetic all-squarefree condition is a natural finite-field Bertini and four-sheeted Hurwitz question; the 3,820 total and 47 source projective orbits give a complete small-field structural classification. The degree-zero/degree-two/degree-three base scheme stratification has direct morphism-theoretic meaning (3,710 genuine degree-four maps). The fourteen six-fibre Frobenius profiles refine the classification by arithmetic splitting of genus-one branch divisors, and the unique complete-splitting-member phenomenon is a nontrivial simultaneous-fibre constraint. These results are not obtainable by simply restating a standard existence theorem.
